summary: This work demonstrates the first experimental setup integrating flux-tunable superconducting qubits and spin ensembles in separate sample volumes within a single dilution refrigerator, achieving magnetic field suppression by more than eight orders of magnitude. The hybrid architecture uses a superconducting NbTi solenoid generating fields up to 50 mT enclosed in layered Cryophy® and superconducting aluminum shields, with verified qubit stability under full field operation.
motivation: Hybrid quantum systems combining superconducting processors with spin-ensemble quantum memories promise enhanced performance, but the incompatibility of operating conditions—spin ensembles require moderate-to-high magnetic fields (300 mT–1.5 T) while superconducting qubits are highly sensitive to magnetic perturbations—presents a major integration challenge that had not been experimentally solved in a single cryogenic environment.
method: Two spatially separated sample volumes 250 mm apart were installed in a Bluefors XLD 1000sl dilution refrigerator: sample volume 1 housed flux-tunable qubits with Cryoperm® shielding, while sample volume 2 contained a superconducting solenoid (4360 turns of 101 µm NbTi wire, inner diameter 70 mm) at 100 mK generating the magnetic field, enclosed in three 1 mm-thick Cryophy® magnetic shields with the outermost replaced by superconducting aluminum. Magnetic field distribution and qubit coherence were characterized via simulation and direct measurement.
result: A flux-tunable qubit with $E_{J1}/h = 16.9$ GHz and $E_{J2}/h = 8.4$ GHz showed no detectable frequency shift or coherence degradation ($T_2^* \approx 1.3$ µs) when the solenoid field was swept through $\pm 50$ mT, corresponding to an attenuation factor of $> 10^8$ at the qubit position. Field homogeneity at the optimal sample position was better than $10^{-4}$ over $\pm 1$ cm radially and $10^{-3}$ over $\pm 10$ mm axially, with thermal load from solenoid operation estimated at 4.2 mW at the 4 K stage.
